after: ## Positivism: why treat society like nature?
alt: Five steps of the scientific method used by positivists: form a hypothesis, collect quantitative data from a large sample, identify patterns and trends, test whether the variables are linked and causal, then accept, reject or refine the hypothesis and publish the method.
caption: Because social facts are external and measurable, positivists study them with the scientific method.

after: ## Positivism: why treat society like nature?
alt: Three panels. A third variable: population size may cause both more police officers and more recorded crime. Reversed direction: reading more may lead to doing well at school, or doing well may lead to reading more. Coincidence: with enough data some variables move together by chance.
caption: Naming one of the three problems scores more than saying "correlation does not prove causation".

alt: Positivism and interpretivism compared. Positivism, linked to Durkheim, sees people as shaped by social facts, takes a macro view, seeks patterns and causes with quantitative data and values objectivity and reliability. Interpretivism, linked to Weber, sees people as conscious actors, takes a micro view, seeks verstehen through qualitative data and values validity.
caption: Each approach follows from a different claim about what society is.

alt: Left: Durkheim used official suicide statistics, found stable rates with Protestant areas higher than Catholic ones, and explained this by social integration. Right: Atkinson argued a death only becomes a suicide statistic after a coroner interprets clues such as a note, the method and recent history, so the figures record decisions.
caption: Positivists treat statistics as facts to explain; interpretivists ask how the statistics were made.

alt: Left: triangulation, shown by Willis’s Learning to Labour (1977), which combined observing lessons, interviews and group discussions to check what twelve working-class boys said against what they did. Right: a longitudinal study follows the same people in waves, such as the Millennium Cohort Study; some drop out at each wave, which is attrition.
caption: Triangulation cross-checks one question with several methods; a longitudinal study returns to the same people.

alt: A table of seven evaluation concepts and the question each asks: bias, interviewer effect, the Hawthorne or observer effect, validity, reliability, representativeness and generalisability. A note explains that the Hawthorne effect is named after research at the Hawthorne works where attention, not conditions, seemed to raise productivity.
caption: Name the concept, then say exactly how it affects the research in front of you.

alt: A four-step plan for evaluating whether sociologists can be objective: introduce by defining objectivity, give points for such as standardised methods and replication, points against such as value-laden topics, interviewer effects and Atkinson’s point about statistics, then judge that bias can be reduced but not removed.
caption: An evaluation answer weighs both sides and ends with a reasoned judgement.
